1202: The variety × storage interaction was non-significant. The highest mean, 0.527 ppm, was recorded for Gobindabhog at 8 months and the lowest, 0.126 ppm, for Kalojira at 12 months. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +0.0% in Gobindabhog, +0.8% in Radhunipagal and -4.6% in Kalojira. The three landraces shifted by nearly equivalent margins, storage having affected them comparably.
1203: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 1.341 ppm was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 0.048 ppm by Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
1212: Iron deficiency ranks among the most prevalent nutritional disorders in India, and since rice is a poor source of the element, any natural variation among rice types merits attention. The elevated iron at Birbhum and Howrah is consistent with the soils of those districts. Aged grain consequently delivers more bioavailable iron than fresh grain, notwithstanding that the total remains unchanged. The same landrace thus returned both a very high and a very low value according to location, which constitutes a strong caution against inferring iron content from a single site. Singh et al. (2022) analysed eleven black, red and white rice cultivars of north-east India and recorded wide ranges in iron, zinc and other minerals alongside phenolic content, the pigmented types proving generally the richer.
1216: Location exerted a highly significant effect on zinc. The highest value, 0.748 ppm, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 0.438 ppm and Birbhum/Howrah with 0.397 ppm. No two locations shared a letter group, each therefore standing apart from the remaining two, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 0.351 ppm.
1218: Varietal differences were equally distinct, attaining significance at the 1% level. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value, 0.708 ppm, followed by Kalojira with 0.486 ppm and Gobindabhog with 0.388 ppm. All three landraces were statistically discrete, Radhunipagal exceeding Gobindabhog by 0.320 ppm.
1220: The effect of storage on zinc was non-significant. In order of sampling, the values were 0.530 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.528 ppm at 4 months, 0.528 ppm at 8 months and 0.524 ppm at 12 months, fresh paddy standing highest and the 12-month sample lowest. By the close of the year the value had declined by 1.1%.
1222: Location and variety did not operate independently, their interaction being highly significant. Radhunipagal at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 1.375 ppm, and Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 0.343 ppm. Rank order varied with location: at Nadia the ranking ran Radhunipagal, Kalojira, Gobindabhog; at Purba Bardhaman, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog. Such reordering establishes that the landraces responded to their environments to differing degrees.
1223: The location × storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean, 0.753 ppm, was recorded for Nadia in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.395 ppm, for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months. By 12 months the three districts had changed by -1.9%, -0.4% and -0.6% respectively. The three locations shifted by nearly equivalent margins, the district of production exerting negligible influence on the action of storage.
1224: No significant interaction emerged between variety and storage. The highest mean, 0.712 ppm, was recorded for Radhunipagal in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.383 ppm, for Gobindabhog at 12 months. The twelve-month change amounted to -2.0% in Gobindabhog, -0.5% in Radhunipagal and -1.3% in Kalojira. All three changed by comparable margins and thus responded to storage in a uniform manner.
1225: The three-factor interaction was significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 1.382 ppm was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 0.333 ppm by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months, a spread of 1.049 ppm. A range of this width arises only from the factors acting in conjunction; the effect proceeded from the three factors together, and all three required appropriate specification to secure the optimum outcome.
1234: Zinc, like iron, is frequently deficient in rice-based diets, and the grain is again a modest source. The two minerals are therefore absorbed and sequestered by at least partially distinct routes within the plant, and none of the three landraces is favourable for both. Zinc absorption is strongly inhibited by phytate, so the improving ratio between the two over twelve months represents a genuine, if modest, nutritional gain that partly offsets the losses recorded in other traits. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal remain scarce. Singh et al. (2022) recorded wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) observed that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati remained stable through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction declined, which corroborates the mineral stability observed here.
1238: Location exerted a highly significant effect on manganese. The highest value, 0.133 ppm, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 0.132 ppm and Nadia with 0.093 ppm. Birbhum/Howrah and Purba Bardhaman shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, while the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 0.040 ppm.
1240: The three landraces also differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value, 0.120 ppm, followed by Gobindabhog with 0.120 ppm and Kalojira with 0.117 ppm. Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog shared a common letter and were thus on par with each other, while Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 0.003 ppm.
1242: The effect of storage on manganese was non-significant. In order of sampling, the values were 0.119 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.119 ppm at 4 months, 0.119 ppm at 8 months and 0.120 ppm at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 12 months and the minimum at 4 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%.
1244: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 0.143 ppm, and Radhunipagal at Nadia the inferior one with 0.088 ppm. The varietal order was not conserved across sites: at Nadia the sequence ran Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; at Purba Bardhaman, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog. Rank reversal of this order establishes that the landraces responded differentially to the three environments.
1245: Location and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean, 0.133 ppm, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months and the lowest, 0.092 ppm, for Nadia at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +0.4% at Nadia, +0.8% at Purba Bardhaman and +0.3% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change scarcely differed between locations, storage having elicited an equivalent response in grain of all three provenances.
1246: The variety × storage term fell short of significance. The highest mean, 0.121 ppm, was recorded for Radhunipagal in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.117 ppm, for Kalojira at 8 months. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +0.7% in Gobindabhog, -0.4% in Radhunipagal and +1.2% in Kalojira. The magnitude of change was comparable in all three landraces, storage having acted upon them equivalently.
1247: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 0.146 ppm was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 0.087 ppm by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
1256: Manganese is a trace element required in small quantities, of which rice grain supplies a useful proportion. In flooded rice soils the availability of manganese is strongly contingent upon the degree of soil reduction and upon pH. Manganese dissolves more readily where a soil remains flooded and anoxic, so differences in the water regimes at the three locations constitute the most plausible explanation for the differentiation observed. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal remain scarce. Singh et al. (2022) recorded wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) observed that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati remained stable through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction declined, which corroborates the mineral stability observed here.
1258: The amino acid profile was determined on freshly harvested grain alone; the samples drawn at 4, 8 and 12 months were not assayed for these parameters. The results presented in this section therefore characterise the influence of location and variety on the amino acids of fresh grain. No inference is drawn regarding the effect of storage, that effect not having been measured. Each table reports the S1 means only, and the SEm and CD figures pertain to the location × variety interaction.
1259: For fourteen of the fifteen amino acids the effect of location was non-significant, proline constituting the sole exception. Varietal differences, by contrast, were highly significant for every amino acid assayed. The amino acid composition of these landraces is therefore determined principally by the genotype and only marginally, if at all, by the district of cultivation.
1260: Gobindabhog carried the greatest quantity of thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, followed by Radhunipagal and, in third position, Kalojira. Two exceptions were recorded: Kalojira contained substantially more cysteine than either of the others and ranked second for tyrosine. Cysteine and tyrosine were barely detectable in Radhunipagal, at 0.0017 and 0.0014 mg/100 mg respectively, values lying at the lower limit of the method's determination.
1264: The effect of location on the histidine content of freshly harvested grain was non-significant, the three locations returning closely comparable values: Nadia recorded 0.1098 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.1088 mg/100 mg and Birbhum/Howrah 0.1087 mg/100 mg.
1266: The three landraces differed distinctly, the varietal effect attaining the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest quantity, 0.1438 mg/100 mg, followed by Radhunipagal at 0.1075 mg/100 mg, with the lowest quantity recorded in Kalojira at 0.0760 mg/100 mg.
1268: No significant location × variety interaction arose, each landrace therefore behaving comparably at all three sites. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Nadia with 0.1451 mg/100 mg and the lowest Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.0753 mg/100 mg. This parameter was determined in fresh grain only, so no storage interaction is reported.
1277: Histidine is an essential amino acid required for growth and haemoglobin synthesis, and it constitutes the precursor from which histamine is formed. The three locations returned almost identical values, from 0.1098 mg/100 mg at Nadia to 0.1087 mg/100 mg at Birbhum and Howrah, an entire spread of 0.0011 mg/100 mg that is far too small to be of consequence. Grain protein composition is determined by the genotype rather than by the soil, so this outcome is the expected one, and Gobindabhog is accordingly the superior of the three on this count. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) placed histidine in rice protein at 1.0 to 3.8% of the total. A grower or buyer may therefore rely upon Gobindabhog to be the richest in histidine wherever it is cultivated in West Bengal.
1281: The effect of location on the serine content of freshly harvested grain was non-significant, the three locations returning closely comparable values: Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.3905 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3897 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.3889 mg/100 mg.
1283: Distinct differences separated the landraces, the varietal effect being highly significant. The largest quantity occurred in Gobindabhog at 0.5544 mg/100 mg, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.3432 mg/100 mg, while Kalojira carried the least at 0.2715 mg/100 mg.
1285: The location × variety term fell short of significance, every landrace behaving consistently across the three districts. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.5563 mg/100 mg and the lowest Kalojira at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.2712 mg/100 mg. No storage samples were assayed for this character; storage interactions are therefore not reported.
1294: Serine is a non-essential amino acid, being synthesisable by the body. It participates in the biosynthesis of lipids and cell membranes and serves as a precursor of glycine and cysteine. The three locations lay within 0.0016 mg/100 mg of one another, from 0.3905 mg/100 mg at Birbhum and Howrah to 0.3889 mg/100 mg at Nadia, and the difference was non-significant. Gobindabhog contained approximately twice the serine of Kalojira, at 0.5544 against 0.2715 mg/100 mg, with Radhunipagal intermediate at 0.3432 mg/100 mg. Serine is abundant in the glutelin fraction, which constitutes the greater part of rice storage protein; a landrace richer in storage protein will therefore manifest a correspondingly higher serine content. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported that glutelin accounts for 79 to 83% of the protein of milled rice, so that its amino acids largely determine the profile of the whole grain.
